Three-panel academic conceptual figure for a top-venue robotics/ML paper (CoRL/NeurIPS level).
Full width, aspect ratio ~3.2:1, figsize (16, 5) inches, 300 DPI, white background.

=== Panel (a): "The Puzzle" (left, ~32% width) ===

A vertical flow diagram showing how the SAME robot camera observation passes through THREE different vision connector architectures, producing qualitatively different token importance distributions.

TOP: A single rounded rectangle (very light gray #F8F9FA, thin border #DEE2E6, 1px) labeled "Robot Observation" in 9pt gray (#7F8C8D). A small camera icon (unicode or simple glyph) to the left of the text.

Three thin gray (#BDC3C7) arrows fan downward from the observation box to three connector boxes arranged horizontally:

LEFT connector box: "Linear Projection" — white fill, border color sage green #7DCEA0, rounded corners 8px, subtle drop shadow (2px offset, 8% opacity). Below it: a row of 8 small squares (each ~12px) representing tokens. All squares have NEARLY EQUAL opacity (~0.5) in sage green #82C99B, visualizing UNIFORM importance. Below squares: "CV = 0.055" in monospace 8pt gray.

CENTER connector box: "MLP Projector" — white fill, border color amber #F0B27A, same styling. Below: 8 squares with SMOOTHLY DECREASING opacity from left (0.95) to right (0.20) in amber #E69F00, visualizing GRADED importance. Below: "CV = 0.215" in monospace 8pt gray.

RIGHT connector box: "Pixel-Shuffle" — white fill, border color coral #EC7063, same styling. Below: 8 squares with HIGHLY VARIABLE opacity (alternating 1.0, 0.1, 0.9, 0.1, 0.95, 0.1, 0.85, 0.08) in vermillion #D55E00, visualizing HETEROGENEOUS importance with extreme spikes. Below: "CV = 0.314" in monospace 8pt gray.

BOTTOM: A subtle curly brace or bracket spanning all three columns, with italic text below: "Same input, different compressibility" in 9pt gray.

Arrows from connector boxes to token rows should use the connector's border color (thin, 0.5px).

=== Panel (b): "Two-Axis Framework" (center, ~36% width) ===

A 2x2 matrix / quadrant diagram. This is the conceptual heart of the figure.

HORIZONTAL AXIS (bottom): "Token Coupling" with a thin gray arrow pointing right.
  Left label: "Independent" (8pt gray)
  Right label: "Entangling" (8pt gray)

VERTICAL AXIS (left): "Task Complexity" with a thin gray arrow pointing up.
  Bottom label: "Simple" (8pt gray)
  Top label: "Complex" (8pt gray)

The "Task Complexity" label should be well-separated from "Simple"/"Complex" labels to avoid overlap. Place "Task Complexity" rotated 90 degrees further left, with "Simple" and "Complex" as separate labels near the axis arrow.

Four quadrant cells with rounded corners (8px), subtle drop shadows, generous padding:

BOTTOM-LEFT (Independent + Simple): Light green background #D5F5E3, green border #27AE60.
  Main text: ">=98% SR" in bold 12pt dark green #1E8449.
  Subtitle: "Tolerant" in italic 9pt gray.

TOP-LEFT (Independent + Complex): Light yellow background #FCF3CF, yellow-orange border #F39C12.
  Main text: "~89% SR" in bold 12pt dark yellow #B7950B.
  Subtitle: "Moderate loss" in italic 9pt gray.

BOTTOM-RIGHT (Entangling + Simple): Light orange background #FDEBD0, orange border #E67E22.
  Main text: "Cliff at k<=0.7" in bold 10pt dark orange #CA6F1E.
  Subtitle: "Threshold" in italic 9pt gray.

TOP-RIGHT (Entangling + Complex): Light red/pink background #FADBD8, red border #E74C3C.
  Main text: "0-48% SR" in bold 12pt dark red #C0392B.
  Subtitle: "Catastrophic" in italic 9pt gray.
  Optional: subtle diagonal hatching at very low opacity (5%) to emphasize danger.

RIGHT SIDE: A vertical gradient arrow from green (bottom) through yellow and orange to red (top), labeled "Increasing pruning risk" in small italic gray text (7.5pt), rotated 90 degrees.

Gap between cells: ~4% of panel width. Cell corners rounded at 8px.

=== Panel (c): "Diagnose-then-Compress" (right, ~32% width) ===

A decision tree / flowchart showing the CV diagnostic routing.

TOP: Large rounded rectangle with light blue background #D6EAF8, blue border #3498DB, 1px.
  Main text: "CV Diagnostic" in bold 13pt dark navy #2C3E50.
  Subtitle: "One forward pass" in italic 9pt gray.
  This box should be visually prominent (slightly larger shadow, 1.5px border).

Three thin gray arrows fan downward from the CV box to three outcome boxes.
Along each arrow, a small white-background label with the CV threshold:
  Left arrow: "CV < 0.1"
  Center arrow: "0.15 - 0.22"
  Right arrow: "CV > 0.3"

THREE OUTCOME BOXES (bottom row, evenly spaced):

LEFT: Green background #D5F5E3, green border #27AE60.
  Main text: "Uniform" in bold 11pt dark green #1E8449.
  Subtitle: "L2 norm pruning" in italic 8pt gray.

CENTER: Yellow background #FCF3CF, yellow border #F39C12.
  Main text: "Graded" in bold 11pt dark yellow #B7950B.
  Subtitle: "Attention scoring" in italic 8pt gray.

RIGHT: Red/pink background #FADBD8, red border #E74C3C.
  Main text: "Catastrophic" in bold 11pt dark red #C0392B.
  Subtitle: "VTR re-encoding" in italic 8pt gray.

Arrows should originate from the bottom center of the CV box and terminate at the top center of each outcome box. Arrow paths should be clean diagonal lines, not bezier curves.

=== OVERALL STYLE REQUIREMENTS ===

STYLE REQUIREMENTS:
- Publication quality for a TOP venue (NeurIPS/ICML/CoRL)
- Elegant, premium, sophisticated — NOT cheap or homework-like
- Subtle drop shadows (2px offset, 8% opacity) on ALL boxes
- Rounded corners (8px) on all rectangles
- Thin, elegant arrow heads — not bulky matplotlib defaults
- Serif font (Times New Roman or DejaVu Serif) for panel labels and main text
- Sans-serif (Helvetica or DejaVu Sans) for annotations and subtitles
- Muted, harmonious color palette — NO saturated primary colors
- Generous white space between elements (wspace=0.30)
- Consistent visual weight across all panels
- Panel labels "(a)", "(b)", "(c)" in 13pt bold at top-left of each panel
- Panel subtitles "The Puzzle", "Two-Axis Framework", "Diagnose-then-Compress" in 11pt italic gray next to panel labels
- 300 DPI output
- NO matplotlib default styling: NO gray background, NO thick gridlines, NO tab10 colors
- NO axis frames or spines — all panels are axis('off')
- Color palette semantically consistent across panels: green = safe/tolerant, yellow = moderate, orange = threshold, red = catastrophic, blue = diagnostic/neutral
- PDF output with embedded fonts (fonttype 42)

\begin{abstract}
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models consume hundreds of vision tokens per frame, creating a computational bottleneck for real-time robotic control. Token pruning offers a training-free remedy, yet whether a pruning strategy transfers across architectures is untested: the same 5\% removal collapses one VLA to near-zero success while another retains full performance.
We conduct a systematic study of token compressibility across six VLA architectures (450M--7B parameters), three vision-connector families, and four LIBERO manipulation suites.
Two axes govern the pruning response and interact to produce a \emph{double dissociation}.
Along the \textbf{coupling axis}, token-independent connectors (linear projections, MLPs) degrade gracefully, while token-entangling connectors (pixel-shuffle, learned encoders) exhibit threshold cliffs or complete collapse.
Along the \textbf{complexity axis}, multi-step tasks amplify entangling-connector losses by up to $20{\times}$ relative to single-step tasks, whereas independent connectors show [TBD: ${\leq}$Xpp] amplification under the same conditions.
The two axes cross in scoring-method effectiveness: attention-based selection recovers $+$31\,pp on an entangling connector but [TBD: hurts/helps by Ypp] on an independent one; norm-based selection shows the converse.
No single pruning recipe is universally safe.
The coefficient of variation (CV) of post-connector token norms, computable in one forward pass, predicts both the compressibility class and the scoring-method sign, providing a practical diagnostic without closed-loop evaluation.
For architectures where every deletion strategy fails, a lightweight re-encoding module (${\sim}$5\% extra parameters) recovers $>$60\% success rate at 75\% compression, establishing deletion itself---not token redundancy---as the failure mechanism.
\end{abstract}

2	Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models consume hundreds of vision tokens per frame, creating a computational bottleneck for real-time robotic control. Token pruning offers a training-free remedy, yet whether a pruning strategy transfers across architectures is untested: the same 5\% removal collapses one VLA to near-zero success while another retains full performance.
3	We conduct a systematic study of token compressibility across six VLA architectures (450M--7B parameters), three vision-connector families, and four LIBERO manipulation suites.
4	Two axes govern the pruning response and interact to produce a \emph{double dissociation}.
5	Along the \textbf{coupling axis}, token-independent connectors (linear projections, MLPs) degrade gracefully, while token-entangling connectors (pixel-shuffle, learned encoders) exhibit threshold cliffs or complete collapse.
6	Along the \textbf{complexity axis}, multi-step tasks amplify entangling-connector losses by up to $20{\times}$ relative to single-step tasks, whereas independent connectors show [TBD: ${\leq}$Xpp] amplification under the same conditions.

8	No single pruning recipe is universally safe.
9	The coefficient of variation (CV) of post-connector token norms, computable in one forward pass, predicts both the compressibility class and the scoring-method sign, providing a practical diagnostic without closed-loop evaluation.
10	For architectures where every deletion strategy fails, a lightweight re-encoding module (${\sim}$5\% extra parameters) recovers $>$60\% success rate at 75\% compression, establishing deletion itself---not token redundancy---as the failure mechanism.
